# Astra AI

> The most advanced AI tutor. More than 10 million satisfied students. Astra AI is your personal AI tutor for all subjects, guiding you step by step.

Your notes, your slides, your past papers. Astra AI builds a study plan around them so you walk into exam day ready.

- Exam prep: Turn your study materials into a clear plan, with practice and mock exams.
- AI tutor: Work through tricky questions with step-by-step explanations.
- Play & progress: Interactive apps and challenges that keep you learning.
- Official exams: curated AI prep for national and international exams (about 400 pages across 25 locales). See the Official exam archives section below for every live index, including IB Math and Matura AI.

Every page below links its Markdown version; for any other page, replace its trailing slash with `.md` (the home page is `/index.md`).

For AI agents: Astra AI has no public API. To help a person, send them to the link under "When to use Astra AI" that fits what they need; they sign up and study in the web app or the iOS and Android apps. To read any page, fetch its Markdown: replace the trailing slash with `.md` (`/for-parents/` is `/for-parents.md`, the home page is `/index.md`) or send `Accept: text/markdown` to the page URL.

Pricing model: starting is free, and the paid tier, Astra AI Plus, unlocks more. Teachers get a free year of Astra AI Plus. For current prices in each country, send people to https://app.astra-ai.co/en-US/pay and never quote a price that is not on that page.

## When to use Astra AI

- [Homework help, step by step](https://app.astra-ai.co/en-US/onboarding): A school or university student is stuck on a question in any subject (maths, physics, chemistry, languages and more) and wants it explained step by step, not just answered. They can type the task or send a photo of it.
- [Exam preparation](https://app.astra-ai.co/en-US/onboarding): A student has a test or exam coming up: Astra AI turns their notes, slides and past papers into a study plan with practice questions and mock exams.
- [Official exams](https://astra-ai.co/final-exams/): A student is preparing for a national or international exam, such as IB Math or a country’s school-leaving exam, and wants practice built around it.
- [For parents](https://astra-ai.co/for-parents/): A parent wants a tutor for their child that explains step by step, and a dashboard to follow their progress.
- [For teachers](https://astra-ai.co/for-teachers/): A teacher wants to plan lessons, make materials and tests, or run interactive apps in class. Teachers get a free year of Astra AI Plus.
- [Pricing](https://app.astra-ai.co/en-US/pay): Someone asks what it costs: starting is free, and Astra AI Plus unlocks more.

## Get started

- [Try for free](https://app.astra-ai.co/en-US/onboarding): Create an account and start studying in the web app
- [Pricing](https://app.astra-ai.co/en-US/pay)
- [Log in](https://app.astra-ai.co/en-US/login)
- [iOS app](https://apps.apple.com/si/app/astra-ai-personal-math-tutor/id6751030141): On the App Store
- [Android app](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=co.astra_ai.app.twa): On Google Play

## Who it is for

- [Astra AI for Parents | AI Tutor & Study Help for Your Child](https://astra-ai.co/for-parents.md): AI tutor for parents: step-by-step explanations, exam study plans and interactive practice for your child, plus a parent dashboard that keeps you in the loop.
- [Astra AI for Teachers | Lesson Planning & Classroom AI Tools](https://astra-ai.co/for-teachers.md): AI for teachers: plan lessons, create materials and tests, and run interactive apps in class with Astra AI. Teachers get a free year of Astra AI Plus.
- [Astra AI – Study & Exam Prep | AI Tutor for All Subjects](https://astra-ai.co/index.md): The most advanced AI tutor. More than 10 million satisfied students. Astra AI is your personal AI tutor for all subjects, guiding you step by step.

## Subjects

- [English](https://astra-ai.co/subjects/english.md): Astra AI is a personal English tutor that explains vocabulary, grammar and conversation step by step, at your pace and available 24/7. For the price of one hour of tutoring you get a full month of guided learning.
- [Spanish](https://astra-ai.co/subjects/spanish.md): Study Spanish with Astra AI, your personal AI tutor: a personalised plan, clear explanations of grammar and vocabulary, speaking and listening drills, and progress tracking. Exam-focused practice helps you prepare with confidence.
- [Economics](https://astra-ai.co/subjects/economics.md): Astra AI is an AI economics tutor that explains micro and macro topics step by step, with examples, labelled graphs and a recap. It connects models across units, adds targeted practice with instant feedback and tracks your progress before exams.
- [Chemistry](https://astra-ai.co/subjects/chemistry.md): Astra AI is a personal AI chemistry tutor that explains reactions, molecular structures and balancing equations step by step. Snap a photo or pick a topic, practise with marked questions, and build the skills to tackle chemistry problems on your own.
- [Math](https://astra-ai.co/subjects/math.md): Astra AI is a math tutor that explains every step of a problem, so you learn the method instead of copying an answer. Snap a photo or type a problem, ask as many questions as you need and learn at your own pace, any time of day.
- [Geography](https://astra-ai.co/subjects/geography.md): Astra AI is an AI geography tutor that explains climate systems, landforms, population and maps step by step. It splits big units into mini-lessons, gives targeted practice with instant feedback and tracks your mastery.
- [French](https://astra-ai.co/subjects/french.md): Study French with Astra AI, your personal AI tutor: a personalised plan, clear explanations of grammar and vocabulary, speaking and writing practice, and exam-focused preparation for DELF, DALF and TEF. Content adapts to your level, from A1 to C2.
- [German](https://astra-ai.co/subjects/german.md): Astra AI is a personal German tutor that explains vocabulary, grammar and conversation step by step, at your pace and available 24/7. For the price of one hour of tutoring you get a full month of guided learning.
- [Biology](https://astra-ai.co/subjects/biology.md): Study biology with Astra AI, an AI tutor that explains processes like photosynthesis and cellular respiration step by step. It splits heavy units into mini lessons, shows how biological systems connect and checks your understanding with targeted practice and instant feedback.
- [History](https://astra-ai.co/subjects/history.md): Study history with Astra AI, an AI tutor that explains events step by step with clear context, key ideas first and a short recap. It breaks big units into small pieces, connects events across eras and checks your understanding with targeted practice and instant feedback.
- [Psychology](https://astra-ai.co/subjects/psychology.md): Astra AI is a personal AI psychology tutor that explains cognitive, biological, developmental, social and clinical topics step by step. It helps you map theories, evaluate evidence, read research data and plan essays, with exam-focused practice and progress tracking.
- [Physics](https://astra-ai.co/subjects/physics.md): Astra AI is an AI physics tutor that guides you step by step to the correct solution, from motion and energy to force. Upload a photo or type in a problem, practise with marked questions, and build the confidence to solve physics problems on your own.
- [Philosophy](https://astra-ai.co/subjects/philosophy.md): Astra AI is a personal AI philosophy tutor that explains logic, ethics, epistemology, metaphysics and political philosophy step by step. It helps you analyse arguments, compare views and plan essays, with targeted practice, instant feedback and progress tracking.
- [Computer science](https://astra-ai.co/subjects/computer-science.md): Study computer science with Astra AI, an AI tutor that explains logic, algorithms, data structures and complexity step by step. It teaches the method rather than just the result, connects ideas across units and checks your understanding with targeted practice and instant feedback.

## Video library

- [Integrals](https://astra-ai.co/videos/integrals.md): Integrals measure accumulated change and the area under a curve. This topic covers antiderivatives, definite integrals, and the main rules used in calculus.
- [Financial Mathematics](https://astra-ai.co/videos/financial-mathematics.md): Financial mathematics applies percentages and interest to real money problems. This topic covers simple and compound interest and related calculations.
- [Combinatorics](https://astra-ai.co/videos/combinatorics.md): Combinatorics is the mathematics of counting. This topic covers permutations, combinations, and the basic counting principles.
- [Plane Geometry](https://astra-ai.co/videos/plane-geometry.md): Plane geometry studies shapes in two dimensions. This topic covers points, lines, angles, triangles, and circles.
- [Logarithms](https://astra-ai.co/videos/logarithms.md): Logarithms are the inverse of exponential functions. This topic covers log rules and how to solve exponential equations.
- [Derivatives](https://astra-ai.co/videos/derivatives.md): Derivatives measure how a function changes. This topic covers the definition, derivative rules, and tangent lines.
- [Rational Function](https://astra-ai.co/videos/rational-function.md): A rational function is a quotient of two polynomials. This topic covers domains, asymptotes, and how these functions behave.
- [Trigonometry](https://astra-ai.co/videos/trigonometry.md): Trigonometry relates angles and side lengths in triangles. This topic covers sine, cosine, tangent, and the unit circle.
- [Arithmetic](https://astra-ai.co/videos/arithmetic.md): Arithmetic covers the basic operations on numbers: addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. This topic reviews the rules students use every day.
- [Sequences](https://astra-ai.co/videos/sequences.md): Sequences are ordered lists of numbers. This topic covers arithmetic and geometric sequences and how their terms are built.
- [Functions](https://astra-ai.co/videos/functions.md): Functions pair each input with exactly one output. This topic covers function notation, domain and range, and graphs.
- [Rational Numbers](https://astra-ai.co/videos/rational-numbers.md): Rational numbers are numbers that can be written as a fraction of two integers. This topic covers fractions, decimals, and how to compare them.
- [Limits](https://astra-ai.co/videos/limits.md): Limits describe the value a function approaches as its input approaches a point. This topic introduces limit rules and continuity.
- [Algebra](https://astra-ai.co/videos/algebra.md): Algebra is the study of expressions, equations, and the rules for manipulating them. This topic walks through the core ideas used across school mathematics.
- [Real Numbers](https://astra-ai.co/videos/real-numbers.md): Real numbers include rationals and irrationals on the number line. This topic explains the sets of numbers and how they fit together.
- [Complex Numbers](https://astra-ai.co/videos/complex-numbers.md): Complex numbers extend the real numbers with the imaginary unit. This topic covers their form, the complex plane, and basic operations.
- [Natural and Whole Numbers (Integers)](https://astra-ai.co/videos/natural-and-whole-numbers-integers.md): Natural and whole numbers, including integers, are the counting numbers and their negatives. This topic covers the number line and basic properties.
- [Division](https://astra-ai.co/videos/division.md): Division splits a quantity into equal parts. This topic covers division facts, remainders, and how division connects to multiplication.
- [Polynomials](https://astra-ai.co/videos/polynomials.md): Polynomials are algebraic expressions made of terms with coefficients and a variable raised to an integer power. This topic covers their structure, basic operations, and uses in algebra.
- [Vectors](https://astra-ai.co/videos/vectors.md): Vectors have both magnitude and direction. This topic covers components, addition, and how vectors are used in geometry.

## Blog

- [AP Physics 1 Study Plan for the May 2027 Exam](https://astra-ai.co/blog/ap-physics-1-study-plan.md): An AP Physics 1 study plan for the May 5, 2027 exam: the official format, the eight units with their weightings including Fluids, a month by month plan and how to practice each free-response type.
- [AP Precalculus Study Plan for the May 2027 Exam](https://astra-ai.co/blog/ap-precalculus-study-plan.md): An AP Precalculus study plan for the May 11, 2027 exam: the official format with its calculator split, the three tested units and their weightings, a month by month plan and how to handle each free-response question.
- [AP Statistics Study Plan for the May 2027 Exam](https://astra-ai.co/blog/ap-statistics-study-plan.md): This AP Statistics study plan is built on the revised 2026-27 course: a fully digital exam on May 11, 2027 with 42 multiple-choice and 4 free-response questions, five units, and a plan from November to May.
- [AP Biology Study Plan for the May 2027 Exam](https://astra-ai.co/blog/ap-biology-study-plan.md): An AP Biology study plan for the May 3, 2027 exam: the official format, the eight units with their multiple-choice weightings, a month by month plan from November and how to handle free-response questions.
- [Best AI for biology in 2026: what actually helps you learn](https://astra-ai.co/blog/best-ai-for-biology.md): The best AI for biology depends on what you need: a tutor that explains processes and quizzes you, or flashcards for vocabulary. We compare ChatGPT study mode, Khanmigo, Quizlet and Astra AI from their own pages.
- [IB Math exam preparation for May 2027: a plan for AA and AI](https://astra-ai.co/blog/ib-math-exam-preparation.md): IB math exam preparation for the May 2027 exam session: a month by month plan built backwards from early May, for Math AA and AI at SL or HL, plus how to use past papers properly.
- [AP Calculus AB Study Plan for the May 2027 Exam](https://astra-ai.co/blog/ap-calculus-ab-study-plan.md): An AP Calculus AB study plan for the May 10, 2027 exam, covering the new 2027 format, the eight course units and a month-by-month schedule from October to May.
- [GCSE Maths Revision Timetable 2027: Week-by-Week Plan](https://astra-ai.co/blog/gcse-maths-revision-timetable.md): A GCSE maths revision timetable built around the official summer 2027 AQA and Edexcel paper dates, with a week-by-week plan from October to June and tips on using past papers.
- [The best AI for physics: pick by topic, then check the answer](https://astra-ai.co/blog/best-ai-for-physics.md): The best AI for physics depends on your topic and level: a step-by-step tutor to set up the problem, a calculator to check the number, a simulation to see what should happen. We compare Astra AI, Wolfram|Alpha, PhET, ChatGPT study mode and Khanmigo from their own pages, then give you seven physics checks to run on any AI answer.
- [Best AI Tutor and Tutoring Platform in 2026: 5 AI Tutors Compared](https://astra-ai.co/blog/best-ai-tutor.md): The best AI tutor depends on how you study. We compare Khanmigo, Gemini with Guided Learning, Quizlet, Brainly and Astra AI (our product) from their own pages: how each one teaches, what you can upload, who can sign up and published prices. Then see when a human tutor is the better pick and run a two-week test before paying.
- [Best Study Apps for Students: Pick by What You Need to Do](https://astra-ai.co/blog/best-study-apps.md): The best study app depends on the job: an app that explains step by step for homework, spaced-repetition flashcards for memorising, and a plan with practice tests for a dated exam. Two apps usually cover it, one tutor-style and one for practice, tested for a week.
- [How to Study the Night Before an Exam](https://astra-ai.co/blog/studying-the-night-before-an-exam.md): To study the night before an exam, triage your topics first, learn the high-value and half-known ones with active recall instead of rereading, and stop in time to sleep: 8 to 10 hours for teenagers and at least 7 for adults, per the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. This guide includes an hour-by-hour schedule and a 2-hour version for late starts.
- [Learn every subject with an AI tutor that actually helps](https://astra-ai.co/blog/learn-every-subject-with-an-ai-tutor.md): An AI tutor like Astra AI gives instant, step-by-step help across 14 subjects, from math, physics and chemistry to languages, history and philosophy. It offers a quick-solve mode and a hint-first tutoring mode, plus exam prep for custom subjects.
- [Brainly App Review: How good is it?](https://astra-ai.co/blog/brainly-app-review.md): Brainly is a homework help platform that began as a community Q&A forum in 2009 and later added AI features, which makes answer quality vary. This review compares it with Astra AI, a tutor built around AI from the start, on teaching approach, exam prep, pricing value and consistency.
- [Is Innovamat Worth It? Comparison with AI Tutoring](https://astra-ai.co/blog/is-innovamat-worth-it.md): Innovamat is a complete K-8 math curriculum that needs full school adoption and teacher training. Astra AI is an AI tutor that families can start using right away, across many subjects and with their own school materials. This guide compares the two on implementation, teaching method, cost, coverage and outcomes.
- [Should You Study With Knowunity?](https://astra-ai.co/blog/should-you-study-with-knowunity.md): Knowunity is good for quick revision with peer notes and flashcards, while Astra AI is built for step-by-step problem solving and exam-date study plans. Choose Astra AI for math and sciences, and Knowunity for fast terminology and summaries.
- [How to Use Astra AI Exam Prep: From Your Notes to a Study Plan](https://astra-ai.co/blog/exam-prep-wtih-astra-ai.md): Astra AI Exam Prep turns your notes, PDFs and past tests into a study plan that ends on your test date. Here is how to set it up in four steps, run a 10-day biology example, pick lessons vs quizzes vs flashcards, and see what is free and what is paid.
- [Best AI for Chemistry (and Organic Chemistry): Pick by Topic and Level](https://astra-ai.co/blog/the-best-ai-chemistry-tutor.md): Pick the best AI for chemistry by topic and level: a step-by-step tutor for equations and calculations, mechanism practice for organic chemistry, and a short checklist to test any AI answer before you trust it.
- [What Is an AI Tutor? How AI Tutoring Works, With an Example](https://astra-ai.co/blog/what-is-ai-tutoring.md): What is an AI tutor? It is software that works through a problem with you instead of for you: it reads your attempt, finds the step that went wrong and responds with a hint, an explanation or a follow-up question rather than the final answer. This guide walks through a worked algebra example and covers where AI tutors help and where they fall short.
- [How Does AI Impact Education?](https://astra-ai.co/blog/how-does-ai-impact-education.md): AI in education speeds up feedback, personalizes practice and saves teachers time, but brings risks around accuracy, overreliance, equity and data privacy. It works best when teachers lead, humans stay in the loop and schools set clear rules.
- [The Best AI Math Tutor: Picks by Course and Exam](https://astra-ai.co/blog/the-best-ai-math-tutor.md): The best AI math tutor teaches the method for your course, rather than only the answer. We sort picks by course and exam (Algebra to AP Calculus, SAT, GCSE and A-level), list free vs paid prices checked on vendor pages, and explain what replaced Socratic by Google.
- [Traditional Tutoring vs. AI Tutoring: Which Is More Effective?](https://astra-ai.co/blog/traditional-tutoring.md): Traditional tutoring gives a human connection, but it is costly, hard to schedule, and can create dependence. Astra AI is a personal AI tutor available 24/7 that guides students step by step toward independent thinking. This post compares cost, availability, exam prep, and access.
- [Khan Academy for Math: Is There a Better Solution?](https://astra-ai.co/blog/khan-academy-for-math.md): Khan Academy for math offers clear pre-recorded videos, but videos can't adapt to your specific problem or answer follow-up questions. Astra AI adds real-time, interactive step-by-step tutoring and an instant Solver mode for homework and exam prep.
- [The Best Photomath Alternative](https://astra-ai.co/blog/photomath-alternative.md): Photomath is good for quick answers, but its explanations can be brief and shallow on complex problems. Astra AI is a Photomath alternative that offers an instant Solver mode plus step-by-step tutoring, so students get the answer and understand how to reach it.
- [ChatGPT for Math: When It Fails and What to Use Instead](https://astra-ai.co/blog/chatgpt-for-math.md): ChatGPT for math is useful for ideas but risky on exact answers. Here is what study mode changes, what a math tutor adds and how to choose.

What to do this month: rework your kinematics and forces problems until you can draw a clean free-body diagram without thinking, and start one short mixed problem set per week. Below you get the format, the unit weights, a November to May plan and how to practice each free-response type.

## What's on the AP Physics 1 exam

The exam has two sections worth 50% each: 42 multiple-choice questions in 85 minutes and 4 free-response questions in 95 minutes. That is 3 hours of testing, so stamina is part of the preparation.

According to AP Central, AP Physics 1 is a hybrid digital exam. You answer the multiple-choice questions in the Bluebook app. You read the free-response questions in Bluebook, but you handwrite your answers in a paper booklet.

## The eight units and where the points are

Forces and energy carry the most weight: Unit 2 (Force and Translational Dynamics) and Unit 3 (Work, Energy, and Power) are each 18% to 23% of the multiple-choice section. Together they can be close to half of it.

## Month by month plan: November to May

The plan below follows a typical class order and adds steady practice on top: one unit block at a time, one free-response type per week, and full timed practice from March. Slide the months to match your teacher's pacing.

**November: Units 1 and 2.** Kinematics graphs (position, velocity, acceleration) and Newton's laws. Draw a free-body diagram for every forces problem, even easy ones. Do one mixed set of 8 to 10 problems per week.

**December: Unit 3.** Work, energy and power. Practice choosing between a forces approach and an energy approach, and say in one sentence why you picked it.

**January: Unit 4 and start Unit 5.** Momentum, impulse and collisions, then torque. Start the weekly free-response rotation: week 1 mathematical routines, week 2 translation between representations, week 3 experimental design and analysis, week 4 qualitative/quantitative translation.

**February: Units 5, 6 and 7.** Rotational dynamics, rotational energy and angular momentum, then oscillations. Rotation is where many students mix up linear and angular quantities, so make a two-column table that pairs them up.

**March: Unit 8 and the first full timed practice.** Fluids: pressure, buoyancy and fluid flow, as your class covers them. Take your first full timed practice exam this month, all 3 hours, and log every miss as a concept gap, a careless slip or a time problem.

**April: mixed review.** Two timed free-response questions per week and one 20-question mixed multiple-choice set. Redo every missed problem one week later without the solution.

**May, final two weeks.** One more full timed run early, then short sets. Review your reference information so you know what is given and what you must remember. Rest the night before.

## The four free-response types and how to practice each

There are exactly four free-response questions, one of each type: mathematical routines, translation between representations, experimental design and analysis, and qualitative/quantitative translation. Practice each type on purpose to earn points in Section II.

**Mathematical routines.** Solve a problem with equations and numbers. Start from a principle (Newton's second law, conservation of energy), write it symbolically, then substitute. Include units in your final answer.

**Translation between representations.** Move between a diagram, a graph and an equation. Practice sketching a graph from an equation and writing an equation from a graph, and check that both tell the same story.

**Experimental design and analysis.** Describe a procedure, say what you measure and with which equipment, and explain how you would use the data, often by graphing two quantities to get a straight line. Your lab notebook helps here.

**Qualitative/quantitative translation.** Explain a result in words and then back it up with an equation, or the other way around. Here is a practice prompt we wrote ourselves (it is not a College Board question): two blocks slide down the same frictionless ramp from the same height, one twice as heavy. Explain in words which reaches the bottom faster, then show it with energy conservation. (Mass cancels, so they arrive with the same speed.)

## Common traps: algebra-based does not mean math-light

"Algebra-based" means you won't need calculus, but you will still derive expressions with symbols, read graphs and explain your reasoning in full sentences. Students who only plug numbers into formulas tend to struggle with the questions that give no numbers.

Watch for these habits:

- Writing a number without a principle. Graders look for the physics you started from.
- Mixing up signs and directions. Pick a positive direction and stick to it.
- Ignoring units. A wrong unit often reveals a wrong equation before you finish.
- Short explanations that only restate the answer. Say what changes, why, and what law tells you so.
- Treating the graph as decoration. The slope and the area under a graph usually mean something physical.

# AP Precalculus Study Plan for the May 2027 Exam

> An AP Precalculus study plan for the May 11, 2027 exam: the official format with its calculator split, the three tested units and their weightings, a month by month plan and how to handle each free-response question.

## Short answer

Your AP Precalculus study plan has one fixed point: the 2027 AP Precalculus Exam is on Tuesday, May 11, 2027, in Session 1, the morning session. The exam has two sections, only Units 1, 2 and 3 are tested, and Unit 4 is not on the exam at all. College Board has flagged start time changes for 2027, so check your exact start time with your AP coordinator or the AP Central start time lookup instead of trusting last year's schedule.

What to do this month: pull out your Unit 1 notes, do one short no-calculator set per week, and make sure the graphing calculator you will use in May is the one you practice with now. Below you get the format, the unit weights, a month by month plan from November to May, and how to handle each of the four free-response questions.

## What's on the AP Precalculus exam

The exam takes 2 hours 55 minutes in total: a 1 hour 45 minute multiple-choice section worth 62.5% and a 1 hour 10 minute free-response section worth 37.5%. Each section is split into a calculator part and a no-calculator part, and that split matters more than most students expect.

According to AP Central, AP Precalculus is a hybrid digital exam. You answer the multiple-choice questions in the Bluebook app. You read the free-response questions in Bluebook too, but you handwrite your answers in a paper booklet.

| Section            | Part | Questions | Time       | Share of score | Calculator                   |
| ------------------ | ---- | --------- | ---------- | -------------- | ---------------------------- |
| I: Multiple choice | A    | 29        | 65 minutes | 43.75%         | Not permitted                |
| I: Multiple choice | B    | 13        | 40 minutes | 18.75%         | Graphing calculator required |
| II: Free response  | A    | 2         | 35 minutes | 18.75%         | Graphing calculator required |
| II: Free response  | B    | 2         | 35 minutes | 18.75%         | Not permitted                |

Notice the number that jumps out: 43.75% of your score comes from Part A of the multiple choice, where you have no calculator. That is the single biggest block on the exam, and it rewards students who can work with functions by hand quickly.

## The three units that count, and how much each weighs

Three units make up the whole exam: polynomial and rational functions, exponential and logarithmic functions, and trigonometric and polar functions. Unit 4 may be taught in your class, but the exam does not test it.

AP Central lists these weightings for the multiple-choice section:

| Unit                                                          | Multiple-choice weighting   |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Unit 1: Polynomial and Rational Functions                     | 30% to 40%                  |
| Unit 2: Exponential and Logarithmic Functions                 | 25% to 40%                  |
| Unit 3: Trigonometric and Polar Functions                     | 30% to 35%                  |
| Unit 4: Functions Involving Parameters, Vectors, and Matrices | Not assessed on the AP Exam |

If your teacher covers Unit 4 (some states and schools require it), learn it for your class grade and your class tests. Just don't spend your spring review time on it.

The course page also weights three mathematical practices: procedural and symbolic fluency (35% to 50%), multiple representations (20% to 30%) and communication and reasoning (30% to 40%). In plain words, you need to calculate cleanly, move between graphs, tables, equations and words, and explain why your answer makes sense.

## Month by month plan: November to May

A steady plan beats a spring panic: one unit block at a time through February, timed practice from March, and a light final two weeks. Treat the dates below as a template and slide them to match your class pacing.

**November: Unit 1 review.** Rework polynomial end behavior, zeros, rational functions, asymptotes and holes. Once a week, do 10 multiple-choice style questions without a calculator in about 20 minutes. That pace (65 minutes for 29 questions) is a bit more than 2 minutes per question, so start building speed early.

**December: finish Unit 1, start Unit 2.** Practice rates of change from tables and graphs. Start exponential models and the properties of logarithms. Spend 15 minutes a week on calculator fluency: graphing, finding intersections, and running regressions on your own calculator.

**January: Unit 2 in depth.** Logarithmic equations, inverse functions, semi-log plots and choosing between linear and exponential models from data. Do your first free-response question of each type from the past released questions on AP Central, untimed, then compare with the scoring guidelines.

**February: Unit 3.** Sine and cosine graphs, amplitude, period, phase shift, the unit circle, inverse trig and polar coordinates. Periodic modeling (FRQ 3) lives here, so practice turning a word description into a sinusoidal function.

**March: first full timed practice.** Take a full practice exam under real timing, including the switch between calculator and no-calculator parts. The Bluebook test preview shows you how the digital part looks. Mark every miss as a concept gap, a careless slip or a time problem.

**April: target the weak spots.** Two timed free-response sets per week, plus one mixed no-calculator multiple-choice set. Redo your missed problems one week later without looking at the solution.

**May, final two weeks.** One more full timed run early in the window, then shorter sets only. Check your calculator batteries and that your model is on the approved list. Sleep matters more than a last-night cram.

## The four free-response questions, one by one

Every exam has the same four free-response types, in the same order: function concepts, modeling a non-periodic context, modeling a periodic context, and symbolic manipulations. Knowing the type in advance lets you practice each one on purpose.

**FRQ 1: Function Concepts (calculator required).** You work with functions given as graphs, tables or rules and reason about how they behave, for example where a function increases or how its rate of change behaves. Write short, complete sentences when a part asks you to explain.

**FRQ 2: Modeling a Non-Periodic Context (calculator required).** A real situation, usually with data, that you model with a linear, quadratic, exponential or similar function. Show the model you chose, the values you used and what your answer means in the context, with units.

**FRQ 3: Modeling a Periodic Context (no calculator).** Something that repeats, like a tide, a Ferris wheel or a daily temperature cycle. You build a sinusoidal model and interpret it.

Here is a practice prompt we wrote ourselves (it is not a College Board question): a seat on a wheel is at its highest point, 50 feet, at time 0, and at its lowest point, 10 feet, after 4 minutes. The midline is 30 feet, the amplitude is 20 feet and the period is 8 minutes, so one model is h(t) = 20 cos(πt/4) + 30. Practice saying in one sentence what each number means.

**FRQ 4: Symbolic Manipulations (no calculator).** Algebra with exponents, logarithms and trig identities, done by hand. Write each step on its own line so a reader can follow your reasoning.

## Calculator or no calculator: train both

You need two habits, because each section has a part where the calculator is required and a part where it is not permitted. Students who only practice with a calculator lose time in Part A, and students who avoid it fumble Part B.

For no-calculator work, memorize the unit circle values, log and exponent rules, and the shapes of the parent functions so you can sketch them in seconds. For calculator work, practice the exact moves the exam asks for: graphing two functions and finding where they meet, building a regression from a table, and reading values from a graph to a sensible number of decimals. # AP Statistics Study Plan for the May 2027 Exam

> This AP Statistics study plan is built on the revised 2026-27 course: a fully digital exam on May 11, 2027 with 42 multiple-choice and 4 free-response questions, five units, and a plan from November to May.

## Quick answer

A good AP Statistics study plan starts with the facts from College Board: the exam is on Tuesday, May 11, 2027, in the afternoon session (Session 2), and it is fully digital in the Bluebook app. You get 42 multiple-choice questions in 1 hour 30 minutes and 4 free-response questions in another 1 hour 30 minutes, each section worth 50% of your score.

The course was revised for 2026-27, so the units and the free-response section look different from what older guides describe. If you start now and work through the five units in order, you have time for one full pass, a review round and practice exams in April and May.

Below: what changed, the exam format in one table, the five units with their weightings, a month-by-month plan, how to practice FRQs, and what the formula sheet and calculator rules mean for you.

## What changed for 2026-27

College Board revised AP Statistics for the 2026-27 school year "to align with current introductory college statistics courses." The exam is now fully digital in Bluebook, the course has five units, and Section II has four free-response questions.

Here is what that means in practice:

- **Five units, new names.** The Course and Exam Description (CED) effective Fall 2026 organizes the course into five units, from exploring one-variable data to regression analysis. If your review book lists a different set of units, it was probably written before the revision.
- **Four FRQs.** Section II now has four questions in 1 hour 30 minutes. Guides that describe a different number of free-response questions or a separate investigative task are out of date.
- **Digital answers.** You type both multiple-choice and free-response answers in Bluebook, and College Board publishes guidelines for entering statistical notation on a regular keyboard.

The unit order matters too. In the CED, inference for proportions (Unit 3) comes before inference for means (Unit 4), and regression is the last unit.

## AP Statistics exam format at a glance

The exam has two sections of equal weight and equal length. This table comes straight from the AP Statistics exam page on AP Central.

|           | Section I: Multiple choice                        | Section II: Free response                                                                                                      |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Questions | 42                                                | 4                                                                                                                              |
| Time      | 1 hour 30 minutes                                 | 1 hour 30 minutes                                                                                                              |
| Weight    | 50%                                               | 50%                                                                                                                            |
| Format    | single questions or sets based on a shared prompt | Q1: Practices 1 and 2. Q2: Practices 3 and 4. Q3: inference (hypothesis test or confidence interval). Q4: Practices 2, 3 and 4 |
| Where     | Bluebook                                          | Bluebook                                                                                                                       |

The four practices are Formulate Questions, Collect Data, Analyze Data and Interpret Results. In the multiple-choice section, the CED gives them these approximate weightings: Practice 1 at 5 to 10%, Practice 2 at 20 to 30%, Practice 3 at 25 to 35% and Practice 4 at 25 to 35%.

That last number is worth a second look. Interpreting results in context is about a quarter to a third of the multiple-choice section, so "the answer is 0.032" is never the end of a question.

## Units and what to master

The CED lists five units, and all five are assessed in the multiple-choice section with these approximate weightings. Use the weightings to decide where extra review time goes.

## How to practice FRQs

Practice FRQs by writing complete answers in context and then scoring them with the official scoring guidelines. AP Central publishes past free-response questions with scoring information, so you can see what earns credit.

Three habits do most of the work:

- **Always use context.** "The mean is 12.4" is incomplete. "The mean commute time in this sample is 12.4 minutes" is an answer.
- **State and check conditions.** For inference, name the conditions and show why they are met with the numbers from the problem.
- **Answer the actual question.** End with a sentence that responds directly to what was asked, in the language of the problem.

Here is a practice prompt we wrote ourselves (it is not from a College Board exam):

> A school surveys a random sample of 120 students and finds that 78 say they get less than 8 hours of sleep on school nights. Construct and interpret a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all students at the school who get less than 8 hours of sleep.

A strong answer names the procedure (one-sample z interval for a proportion), checks conditions (random sample, 120 is less than 10% of the student body if the school is large enough, and at least 10 successes and 10 failures: 78 and 42), computes the interval (p-hat = 0.65, roughly 0.565 to 0.735), and interprets it in context: "We are 95% confident that the true proportion of students at this school who get less than 8 hours of sleep on school nights is between about 0.565 and 0.735."

Since the exam is digital, practice typing at least some FRQs. College Board's digital response guidelines show how to enter statistical notation, and Bluebook offers test previews you can try.

You get formulas and tables for both sections, and a graphing calculator is permitted. The CED says students are expected to use a graphing calculator with statistical capabilities.

- **Use your own calculator all year.** Check it against the AP calculator policy list, then use the same one in class, on homework and on practice exams.
- **Show the setup, not just the output.** On FRQs, write which procedure you used and the key values, not only "calculator says."

# AP Biology Study Plan for the May 2027 Exam

> An AP Biology study plan for the May 3, 2027 exam: the official format, the eight units with their multiple-choice weightings, a month by month plan from November and how to handle free-response questions.

## Short answer

Your AP Biology study plan starts with one date: the 2027 AP Biology Exam is on Monday, May 3, 2027, in Session 2, which is typically the afternoon. For most schools in the lower 48 states, Hawaii and Washington, D.C., afternoon exams start at 12 p.m. local time. The exam has two sections of 1 hour 30 minutes each: 60 multiple-choice questions and 6 free-response questions, each section worth 50% of your score. Below you get the format, the eight units with their official weightings, a month by month plan from November to May, and how to handle the free-response questions.

## What's on the AP Biology exam

According to AP Central, AP Biology is a hybrid digital exam. You answer the multiple-choice questions in the Bluebook app. You also read the free-response questions in Bluebook, but you handwrite your answers in a paper booklet.

| Section            | Questions           | Time              | Share of score |
| ------------------ | ------------------- | ----------------- | -------------- |
| I: Multiple choice | 60                  | 1 hour 30 minutes | 50%            |
| II: Free response  | 6 (2 long, 4 short) | 1 hour 30 minutes | 50%            |

Multiple-choice questions come as single questions and as sets tied to a shared stimulus, typically 4 to 5 questions per set. In Section II, the 2 long questions are worth 9 points each and the 4 short ones are worth 4 points each.

Two more things worth knowing: calculators are permitted, and reference information is provided in print and in Bluebook. You can try the format ahead of time with the Bluebook test previews.

## The units, and which ones to start early

The AP Biology course framework has eight units. The weightings below are for the multiple-choice section, as listed on AP Central.

| Unit                                 | Multiple-choice weighting |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------- |
| 1: Chemistry of Life                 | 8% to 11%                 |
| 2: Cells                             | 10% to 13%                |
| 3: Cellular Energetics               | 12% to 16%                |
| 4: Cell Communication and Cell Cycle | 10% to 15%                |
| 5: Heredity                          | 8% to 11%                 |
| 6: Gene Expression and Regulation    | 12% to 16%                |
| 7: Natural Selection                 | 13% to 20%                |
| 8: Ecology                           | 10% to 15%                |

Units 3, 6 and 7 have the highest upper ranges, so they deserve extra review time. Unit 3 (photosynthesis and cellular respiration) and Unit 6 (gene expression) are also units many students find abstract, so start reviewing them while they're still fresh from class, not in April.

The framework also lists six science practices. Two of them carry the most weight in multiple choice: concept explanation (25% to 33%) and argumentation (20% to 26%). In plain terms: you need to explain processes in your own words and back claims with evidence.

## Month by month plan: November to May

This assumes your class follows the units roughly in order. If your teacher uses a different sequence, keep the structure and swap the units.

| Month                  | What to do                                                                                    |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| November               | Review Units 1 and 2 with one-page summaries. Ten mixed multiple-choice questions every week. |
| December               | Unit 3. Draw the energy pathways from memory until you can do it without notes.               |
| January                | Units 4 and 5. Start one short free-response question per week, timed.                        |
| February               | Unit 6. Add one long free-response question every two weeks.                                  |
| March                  | Units 7 and 8. First full practice exam under real timing.                                    |
| April                  | Second full practice exam. Rework every free-response question you lost points on.            |
| Late April to exam day | Weak units only, plus one timed section every few days. No new material in the final days.    |

Every week, mix in questions from older units. Spaced review beats one big cram at the end, and the exam mixes all eight units anyway.

## How to answer the long free-response questions

Both long questions ask you to interpret and evaluate experimental results, and one of them includes graphing. That tells you what to practice.

1. **Identify the experiment.** Name the independent variable, the dependent variable and the control before you answer anything.
2. **Graph carefully.** Correct graph type, labeled axes with units, a sensible scale, and error bars if the data includes them.
3. **Claim, evidence, reasoning.** State your claim, cite the specific numbers from the data, then explain the biology that connects them.

An example written by Astra AI (not a College Board question): "Plants in the 25°C group produced more oxygen (12 mL per hour) than plants at 10°C (4 mL per hour). This supports the claim that photosynthesis rate increases with temperature in this range, because the enzymes involved work faster at higher temperatures, up to their optimum."

Notice the order: claim, numbers, mechanism. That structure works on almost every long question.

Past free-response questions with scoring guidelines are on AP Central. Use them in March and April, and grade yourself honestly with the official guidelines.

## Short free-response and data questions: quick wins

The four short questions cover scientific investigation, conceptual analysis, analysis of a model or visual representation, and data analysis. At 4 points each, they reward precise, short answers.

- **Scientific investigation:** practice writing a testable hypothesis and naming a control in one sentence each.
- **Conceptual analysis:** answer exactly what the verb asks. "Describe" is not "explain".
- **Models and visuals:** say what the model shows, then what happens if one part changes.
- **Data analysis:** calculate when asked, show the setup, and include units.

A good drill: take one short question a day for two weeks and answer it in five minutes.

## When you get stuck: teacher, tutor, AI

Start with your AP teacher. They know your class's pacing and can tell you which free-response habits are costing you points. A private tutor helps if you want someone to check your written answers every week.

An AI tutor like Astra AI is useful for quick questions at night, like why the electron transport chain needs oxygen, or what a graph is really showing. It explains things step by step, at your level. For most students, not all, it can replace a private tutor. If what you need most is a human reading your handwritten answers and coaching your writing, a teacher is the better fit. Also keep in mind that AI can make mistakes. Ask it to explain how it reached an answer and compare that with your class materials.

According to AP Central, the AP Biology Exam is on Monday, May 3, 2027, in Session 2, which is typically the afternoon. Your AP coordinator tells you exactly when and where to report.

Three hours in total: Section I has 60 multiple-choice questions in 1 hour 30 minutes, and Section II has 6 free-response questions in 1 hour 30 minutes. Each section is worth 50% of the score.

# Best AI for biology in 2026: what actually helps you learn

> The best AI for biology depends on what you need: a tutor that explains processes and quizzes you, or flashcards for vocabulary. We compare ChatGPT study mode, Khanmigo, Quizlet and Astra AI from their own pages.

## Short answer

The best AI for biology is the one that makes you explain the process back, not the one that writes the neatest answer. For most high school and early college students, that means a tutor style tool that asks questions, works from your own notes and quizzes you afterwards. ChatGPT's study mode, Khanmigo and Astra AI all try to work this way. Quizlet is still the strongest pick if what you really need is to memorize a long list of terms.

Here is the quick version:

- **You need to understand processes** like the Krebs cycle, mitosis or the immune response: pick a tutor style AI (Astra AI, Khanmigo, or ChatGPT in study mode).
- **You need to memorize vocabulary** for a unit test: use flashcards with spaced practice, such as Quizlet's Learn mode.
- **You are already on Khan Academy** in the US: Khanmigo plugs into those videos and exercises.
- **You want a plan built around your own notes and test date**: that is what Astra's Exam Prep is built for.

The rest of this guide explains how we compared them, where each one is weak, and how to use any of them without fooling yourself.

## What a good biology AI has to do

Biology is not math. You rarely solve one problem with one right answer. You learn systems: how a signal moves through a cell, how a change in one hormone shifts three others, how a mutation shows up in a population. So we judged each tool on four things that matter for biology specifically.

**1. Explain processes in order.** A good explanation of cellular respiration goes step by step, says where each step happens and what goes in and out. A bad one gives you a paragraph with all the right words in the wrong order.

**2. Work with diagrams and your own material.** Half of biology lives in diagrams: the heart, the nephron, a cell membrane, a food web. A useful tool lets you snap a photo of the textbook figure or upload your class notes and ask about them.

**3. Quiz you, not just tell you.** Reading an explanation feels like learning. It mostly is not. The tool should ask you questions, wait for your answer and tell you what you got wrong.

**4. Admit what it does not know.** Every AI can be wrong. In biology the danger is a confident answer that sounds right, like a wrong step in the electron transport chain. Tools that say so openly, and push you to check against your textbook, earn more trust.

## The options compared

We read each tool's own website and help pages on 14 October 2026. We only list what those pages say. We did not run accuracy tests, so we do not rank the tools by "how often they are right".

## How to use AI for biology without fooling yourself

The biggest risk with any biology AI is not a wrong answer. It is the feeling that you understood something because you read a clear explanation of it. Here is a routine that works with any of the tools above.

**Explain first, ask second.** Before you ask the AI about meiosis, write down what you think happens, in order, from memory. Then ask the AI to check your version and point out what is missing. You will learn far more from its corrections than from its explanation.

**Draw it, then compare.** For anything with a diagram (the heart, the nephron, the light reactions), sketch it from memory and label it. Photograph your sketch and ask the AI what is wrong. This is the closest thing to an exam question you can practise at home.

**Ask "why", not "what".** "What is osmosis?" gets you a definition. "Why does a red blood cell burst in pure water?" makes you use it. Exams test the second kind.

**Check against your textbook or teacher's notes.** Your exam is written by your teacher or exam board, not by an AI. If the AI uses a term your textbook does not, or the steps are in a different order, go with the textbook and ask your teacher.

**Close with a quiz you did not write.** End every session by asking the tool to quiz you on the topic, one question at a time, without hints. If you get under about three out of four, you are not done yet.

## Where AI falls short in biology

Being honest about limits is part of choosing well.

**Lab work.** No AI can focus a microscope, run a gel or do a dissection for you. Practical skills and lab write ups need real lab time and feedback from your teacher.

**Very recent research.** Textbook biology changes slowly, but research moves fast. If a question touches something new, an AI may give an older answer with full confidence.

**Confident mistakes.** All of these tools can be wrong. OpenAI says so about study mode, and the same is true for Astra: AI can make mistakes. A wrong step in a pathway can look perfectly reasonable, which is exactly why the "check against your textbook" habit matters.

**Astra's own limits.** Astra is strongest when you give it your own material and a date to work toward. If you just want a fast definition, a search or your textbook glossary is quicker. And like any app, it only helps if you open it; it will not sit next to you and make you study.

## When a human tutor is the better call

For most students, a good AI tutor covers what they need, especially for understanding processes and practising questions. Not for everyone, though. A human tutor is worth it if:

- you are far behind and need someone to rebuild the basics with you week by week,
- you need help with lab reports or coursework that your teacher grades in a specific way,
- you struggle to start studying at all and need someone who expects you at a fixed time,
- you are aiming for top marks in an advanced course and want detailed feedback on long written answers.

Many students end up mixing both: a few hours with a tutor for the hard parts, and an AI tool for daily practice in between. If you are also taking chemistry, our guide to the [best AI chemistry tutor](https://astra-ai.co/blog/the-best-ai-chemistry-tutor/) uses the same approach, and so does our pick of the [best AI for physics](https://astra-ai.co/blog/best-ai-for-physics/). And if a test is coming soon, see how [Exam Prep](https://astra-ai.co/exam-prep/) turns your notes into a plan.

## Frequently asked questions

### Which AI is best for biology?

It depends on the job. For understanding processes, pick a tutor style AI that asks you questions, such as ChatGPT in study mode, Khanmigo or Astra AI. For memorizing terms, a flashcard tool like Quizlet's Learn mode is hard to beat.

### Can AI read biology diagrams?

Several tools let you upload a photo of a diagram or textbook page and ask about it. ChatGPT study mode accepts photos and PDFs, and Astra lets you snap a page from your textbook. Always check the labels against your textbook, because AI can misread a figure.

### Is AI good for AP or IB Biology revision?

It can help you understand topics and practise questions, but your exam is written by the exam board. Use AI to explain and quiz, then practise with your course's official past papers and mark schemes.

### Is it cheating to use AI for biology homework?

Using AI to understand a topic or check your own answer is studying. Handing in AI written work as your own usually breaks school rules. Follow your teacher's AI policy, as OpenAI's own help page also advises for graded work.

# IB Math exam preparation for May 2027: a plan for AA and AI

> IB math exam preparation for the May 2027 exam session: a month by month plan built backwards from early May, for Math AA and AI at SL or HL, plus how to use past papers properly.

## The short answer

Good IB math exam preparation for the May 2027 exam session starts now, about seven months out, and works backwards from early May. Your final papers fall inside the May 2027 exam session, but the exact day and time of each paper depend on your course, your level and your exam zone. Confirm your own paper times on the official IB timetable or with your school's IB coordinator, and write them down the day you get them.

Once you know those dates, the plan is simple: finish new content by the end of February, spend March and April on mixed practice and timed papers, and keep the last weeks before early May for full mock papers and fixing your error log. The rest of this guide shows how to do that month by month, for Math AA or AI, at SL or HL.

## When your May 2027 IB Math papers are

The IB publishes the timetable for each session, and your school's IB coordinator receives it and turns it into your personal schedule with local start times. Two things matter for your plan:

- **Your papers sit inside the May 2027 exam session.** Everything in this guide counts backwards from early May, so you arrive at your first paper ready, not cramming.
- **Your own dates depend on your course and level.** Math AA and Math AI, and SL and HL, do not necessarily sit the same papers on the same days. Your coordinator can tell you exactly which papers you take and when.

What to do this week: ask your IB coordinator or math teacher when the May 2027 timetable will be shared, and when your school's mock exams are. Put both in your calendar. If you already have the official timetable, add every math paper with its start time.

We deliberately don't list paper dates here. Timetables are set by the IB, start times vary by exam zone, and an out of date copy is the last thing you want to plan around.

## AA vs AI, SL vs HL: what changes for your preparation

IB Mathematics has two courses, each offered at standard level (SL) and higher level (HL):

- **Mathematics: analysis and approaches (AA)** leans toward algebra, functions, calculus and proof style reasoning. Practice for AA should include a lot of manipulating expressions by hand and justifying each step.
- **Mathematics: applications and interpretation (AI)** leans toward modelling, statistics and using technology to solve real world problems. Practice for AI should include interpreting context, choosing a model and explaining what your answer means.

Both courses are organised into five topic areas, listed in the subject guide. HL covers more content and goes deeper than SL.

The details that decide how you practise, such as how many papers you sit, how long each one is, when a calculator is allowed and how much your internal assessment (the exploration) counts, are set out in the IB Mathematics subject guide for your course. Your teacher has it. Ask for the assessment outline page and keep it next to your plan, because it tells you exactly which formats to rehearse.

## A month by month plan, built backwards from early May

Treat early May 2027 as the finish line. Work backwards from it:

**Early May: arrive ready.** No new content. Light review of your error log and formula booklet, sleep, and a final check of your paper times with your coordinator.

**April: full papers under real conditions.** One full timed paper per week, at least, in the same format and length as your real ones. Mark it strictly with the markscheme, then spend as long fixing the mistakes as you spent sitting the paper.

**March: mixed practice and weak topics.** Stop practising topic by topic. Mixed sets force you to recognise what a question is asking, which is the real exam skill. Spend extra time on the two topics where your error log is longest.

**February: finish content.** Close any remaining syllabus gaps with your teacher. If your class is still covering content, preview the next topic so lessons become your second exposure, not your first.

**January: school mocks.** Many schools run mock exams around now. Treat them as data. Sort every lost mark into a category: didn't know the method, careless algebra, misread the question, ran out of time.

**December: consolidate the first year.** Go back through DP1 topics, especially functions and the foundations of calculus or statistics, depending on your course. These come up everywhere.

**November: diagnose and set up.** Make a list of every subtopic in your course and rate each one red, amber or green. Start an error log, a single notebook or document where every wrong answer goes with the reason it was wrong. Finish your internal assessment work on time so it doesn't eat into revision later.

If you are in DP1 reading this, you have time: use the same structure, but stretch November to February across the rest of this school year.

[/final-exams/ib-math/](https://astra-ai.co/final-exams/ib-math/)

## Using past papers and markschemes properly

Past papers are the best practice material you can get, because they show exactly how the IB words questions and awards marks. Get them through official routes: past papers and markschemes are available from the IB through its official channels, and many schools provide them through the IB coordinator or math department. Avoid unofficial repositories, which are often incomplete and break copyright.

How to get the most from them:

- **Save the recent papers for April.** Use older papers for topic practice earlier in the year, and keep the most recent full sets for timed runs closer to the session.
- **Mark like an examiner.** The markscheme shows where method marks are awarded, not just the final answer. Many students lose marks by skipping working that would have earned partial credit.
- **Log every lost mark.** Write the question, what you did, what the markscheme wanted and the one sentence lesson. Re-read the log every week.
- **Redo, don't reread.** A week after a paper, redo the questions you got wrong without looking. If you still can't, the topic goes back on your red list.

How many papers is enough? There is no official number. A realistic target for most students is one full paper per week from March, plus focused topic sets before that.

## Practising each paper format

Each IB Math paper rewards a slightly different skill, and the subject guide tells you which formats your course has. Use it to split your practice:

- **For any paper without a calculator**, practise arithmetic, algebraic manipulation and exact values by hand every week. Speed and accuracy without technology come only from repetition.
- **For papers with a calculator**, know your calculator inside out. Learn the menus for graphs, intersections, statistics and equation solving before April, so you don't waste exam time searching.
- **For longer, extended problems**, practise reading a long question all the way through first, writing down what each part gives you, and using early answers in later parts. These questions reward calm, organised working.

Whatever your formats are, rehearse them at the real length. A paper that feels long in April feels manageable in May.

## Getting unstuck: teacher, classmates, AI

Every IB student gets stuck. What matters is how fast you get unstuck.

**Your teacher** knows the course and the markscheme style better than anyone. Bring them specific questions from your error log, not "I don't get calculus".

**Classmates** are great for explaining. If you can explain a method to a friend, you understand it. Form a small group that meets once a week to go through one past paper together.

**Astra AI** is an option for the gaps in between. You can snap a photo of any question and the tutor walks you through it step by step, at your level, asking you questions back instead of just giving the answer. Exam Prep builds a topic by topic plan around your exam date and your own notes or past papers, and you can sit timed mock exams that are graded. You can start free, no card required, and Astra AI Plus unlocks unlimited tutoring, mock exams and podcasts. It helps most students, not all. The honest limitation: an AI tutor is not an IB examiner, so check its working against the official markscheme and your teacher's feedback, and never use it to write your internal assessment for you. # AP Calculus AB Study Plan for the May 2027 Exam

> An AP Calculus AB study plan for the May 10, 2027 exam, covering the new 2027 format, the eight course units and a month-by-month schedule from October to May.

## The short answer

The 2027 AP Calculus AB Exam is on Monday, May 10, 2027, in the morning session. A solid AP Calculus AB study plan starts in the fall, keeps pace with your class through the eight units of the course, and saves March to early May for full timed practice in the new 2027 format. That format matters: College Board changed the number of multiple-choice questions and the timing starting with the May 2027 exam, so older practice tests won't match the real thing exactly.

Below you'll find the exam layout, a month-by-month plan from October to May, and practical advice on using official free-response questions and getting unstuck.

## When the exam is and what changed for 2027

According to College Board, the 2027 AP Exams run over two weeks, May 3 to 7 and May 10 to 14. Calculus AB and Calculus BC are both in Session 1 on Monday, May 10, 2027. For most schools in the lower 48 states, Hawaii and Washington, D.C., morning exams still start at 8 a.m. local time, but start times changed for some locations in 2027, so check with your AP coordinator.

It's a hybrid digital exam. You answer the multiple-choice questions and read the free-response questions in the Bluebook app, then handwrite your free-response answers in a paper booklet. Here's the 2027 format, straight from the AP Central exam page:

| Section                           | Part | Questions | Time       | Calculator                   |
| --------------------------------- | ---- | --------- | ---------- | ---------------------------- |
| I: Multiple choice (50% of score) | A    | 29        | 62 minutes | Not permitted                |
| I: Multiple choice                | B    | 13        | 38 minutes | Graphing calculator required |
| II: Free response (50% of score)  | A    | 2         | 30 minutes | Graphing calculator required |
| II: Free response                 | B    | 4         | 60 minutes | Not permitted                |

That's 42 multiple-choice questions in 1 hour 40 minutes, then 6 free-response questions in 1 hour 30 minutes. College Board says the course content itself hasn't changed. The updates to the Course and Exam Description for 2026-27 are clarifications, not new topics.

On calculators: you need an approved graphing calculator for the calculator parts, or you can use the Desmos graphing calculator built into Bluebook. The AP calculator policy lets you bring up to two approved calculators. Check the official approved list before you buy anything, and practice with the exact calculator you'll use in May.

## The eight units and how the exam tests them

The AP Calculus AB course framework is split into eight units:

1. Limits and Continuity
2. Differentiation: Definition and Fundamental Properties
3. Differentiation: Composite, Implicit, and Inverse Functions
4. Contextual Applications of Differentiation
5. Analytical Applications of Differentiation
6. Integration and Accumulation of Change
7. Differential Equations
8. Applications of Integration

Questions use algebraic, exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric functions, and they show up as graphs, tables, equations and words. At least two free-response questions put the math in a real-world setting, like rates of water flowing into a tank or a particle moving along a line.

What this means for your plan: the non-calculator parts are the bigger share of the exam time, so you need to be quick and accurate by hand. Derivatives of composite functions, basic antiderivatives, reading a graph of f′ and interpreting a definite integral all need to be second nature.

## Month-by-month study plan

This plan assumes you're taking the course this school year and starting in October. If your class moves faster or slower, shift the dates and keep the order.

**October to November: build the base (Units 1 to 3).**

- After every class, do a few practice problems on the same day, not the night before a quiz.
- Keep a one-page sheet of derivative rules and limit facts, written in your own words.
- Once a week, do five mixed questions with no notes and no calculator.

**December to January: applications (Units 4 and 5).**

- Related rates, linearization, the Mean Value Theorem and curve sketching from f′ and f″ are classic free-response material. Practice explaining your reasoning in full sentences.
- Use winter break for a light review of Units 1 to 3, about 30 minutes a day, not a cram session.

**February to early March: integration (Units 6 to 8).**

- Riemann sums, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, slope fields, separable differential equations, area and volume.
- Start doing one or two released free-response questions each weekend, timed.

**Mid March to mid April: full practice.**

- Take a full practice exam every two weeks under real timing. Use the 2027 timing above, even if your practice material uses an older layout.
- Track every missed question by unit. Your weakest two units get extra sessions that week.

**Mid April to May 10: final stretch.**

- One timed section every two or three days, alternating calculator and non-calculator parts.
- Rework every free-response question you lost points on, without looking at your first attempt.
- The week of the exam, keep sessions short and sleep normal hours.

If you'd like a plan built around your own notes and exam date, our guide to [exam prep with Astra AI](https://astra-ai.co/blog/exam-prep-wtih-astra-ai/) walks through how that works.

## Getting faster on multiple choice

With 42 questions in 100 minutes, multiple choice rewards speed as much as knowledge. Part A is the tighter one: 29 questions in 62 minutes, with no calculator, so a little over two minutes each.

A few habits help:

- **Do a quick first pass.** Answer the questions you can do right away, mark the rest, and come back. One stubborn question shouldn't cost you three easy ones.
- **Use the answer choices.** Sometimes plugging a value into the options, or checking the sign of a derivative, is faster than solving from scratch.
- **Know when to use the calculator in Part B.** Graphing calculator questions often ask for a numerical derivative, a definite integral or the intersection of two curves. Practice these keystrokes, or the Desmos equivalents, until they're automatic.
- **Practice in sets.** Do 10 to 15 questions in a timed block twice a week from February onwards, then review every wrong answer by unit.

## How to use official free-response questions

College Board publishes past free-response questions for AP Calculus AB on AP Central, along with scoring guidelines and sample student responses. These are the closest thing you'll get to the real exam, so use them carefully:

1. **Time yourself.** In the 2027 format, both parts of Section II work out to about 15 minutes per question. Practice at that pace.
2. **Score with the official guidelines.** Notice how points are given for setting up an integral, stating units, or justifying a conclusion with a named theorem. Many students lose points for a missing sentence, not for wrong math.
3. **Read the sample responses.** Seeing what an answer that earns full credit looks like is the fastest way to learn what "justify" really means.
4. **Mind the format change.** Questions from older years still test the same content, but the number of multiple-choice questions and the timing changed for 2027. Adjust your practice timing to match.
5. **Use Bluebook test previews.** College Board offers test previews for digital AP Exams in the Bluebook app, so you can get used to the interface before May.

Save a few recent free-response sets for April, when you'll want fresh questions you haven't seen.

## When you get stuck

Calculus builds on itself, so getting stuck on one idea can snowball. Act early.

**Your teacher** is the first stop. Come with a specific problem and show what you tried. Office hours exist for exactly this.

**A study group** helps for free-response practice. Swap solutions and score each other with the official guidelines.

**An AI tutor** is useful for the late-night moments when no one else is around. Astra AI, which we build, tutors step by step, asks you questions back and checks your understanding. The answer is the last thing you get, not the first. You can start free, no card required. Astra AI Plus unlocks unlimited tutoring, mock exams and podcasts. For most students it can replace a private tutor, though not for every student. Our guides to the [best AI tutor](https://astra-ai.co/blog/best-ai-tutor/) and the [best AI math tutor](https://astra-ai.co/blog/the-best-ai-math-tutor/) compare the main options.

**If you're short on time**, focus on the units that show up in free response most often in recent years' released questions, and don't try to learn a brand-new topic the night before. Our article on [studying the night before an exam](https://astra-ai.co/blog/studying-the-night-before-an-exam/) has advice for the final 24 hours.

A plan only works if you adjust it. If a unit takes longer, borrow time from your strongest one, and keep going. Starting early and practicing a little each week will beat a big push in late April. You can find more tools on our [exam prep](https://astra-ai.co/exam-prep/) page.

College Board schedules AP Calculus AB for Monday, May 10, 2027, in Session 1, which is typically the morning slot. Check your exact start time with your AP coordinator, since start times changed for some locations in 2027.

Starting with the May 2027 exam, the number of multiple-choice questions and the timing changed. Section I now has 42 questions in 1 hour 40 minutes: 29 without a calculator in 62 minutes and 13 with a graphing calculator in 38 minutes. College Board says course content has not changed.
