# GCSE Maths Revision Timetable 2027: Week-by-Week Plan

> A GCSE maths revision timetable built around the official summer 2027 AQA and Edexcel paper dates, with a week-by-week plan from October to June and tips on using past papers.

## The short answer

A good GCSE maths revision timetable works backwards from three fixed dates. If you sit AQA or Pearson Edexcel in summer 2027, Paper 1 (non-calculator) is on Friday 14 May, Paper 2 (calculator) on Thursday 27 May and Paper 3 (calculator) on Monday 14 June, all in the morning and all 1 hour 30 minutes long. Foundation and Higher sit on the same days. That gives you roughly seven months from mid October, which is plenty if you split it into phases: fix the basics before Christmas, use your mocks to find gaps, then move to timed past papers from spring onwards.

The rest of this guide turns that into a week-by-week plan you can stick on your wall, plus a few honest tips on what to do when a topic just won't go in.

## When the 2027 papers fall

Both big exam boards published their final summer 2027 timetables, and for maths they line up exactly:

| Paper   | Calculator? | Date                 | Session | Length |
| ------- | ----------- | -------------------- | ------- | ------ |
| Paper 1 | No          | Friday 14 May 2027   | Morning | 1h 30m |
| Paper 2 | Yes         | Thursday 27 May 2027 | Morning | 1h 30m |
| Paper 3 | Yes         | Monday 14 June 2027  | Morning | 1h 30m |

These dates come from the AQA timetable for GCSE Mathematics (8300) and the Pearson Edexcel GCSE Summer 2027 Final Timetable for Mathematics (1MA1). The links are in the sources at the bottom of this page.

If your school enters you for OCR (J560), check OCR's own published timetable rather than assuming the same days. And whichever board you sit, your exams officer has the final word on rooms and start times, so ask them if anything looks odd. JCQ also keeps a page of key dates and links to every board's timetable.

Two things jump out from the table. First, the non-calculator paper comes first, so mental methods and written arithmetic need to be sharp by early May, not late May. Second, there's a gap of nearly two weeks between Paper 1 and Paper 2, and another two and a half weeks before Paper 3. Those gaps are revision time, and a good plan uses them on purpose.

## Foundation vs Higher and the three papers

You'll sit either Foundation or Higher tier for all three papers. Foundation covers grades 1 to 5 and Higher covers grades 4 to 9. Your teacher usually decides your tier after mocks, so if you're on the borderline, have that conversation early. It changes which topics deserve your time.

All three papers can test any part of the specification. There's no "algebra paper" or "geometry paper", so don't fall into the trap of revising one area per paper. What does change is the calculator rule:

- **Paper 1 (non-calculator).** Fractions, percentages without a calculator, long multiplication and division, surds and exact values on Higher, estimating. Speed and accuracy with written methods matter most here.
- **Papers 2 and 3 (calculator).** Same content, but questions can lean on messier numbers, trigonometry, compound interest, standard form and statistics where a calculator helps. Know your own calculator well: fractions button, memory, powers and roots.

A useful habit is to label each past paper question you get wrong with its topic, not its paper. After a few weeks you'll see your real weak spots, and those are what your timetable should chase.

## Week-by-week timetable

This plan assumes you start in mid October 2026 with about 30 weeks to go until Paper 1. If you start later, squeeze the early phases rather than cutting the past paper phase. Three or four focused maths sessions a week is enough for most students, around 30 to 45 minutes each, with one longer session at the weekend.

**Phase 1: mid October to mid December (about 9 weeks). Rebuild the foundations.**

- Make a topic list from your board's specification and rate each topic red, amber or green.
- Spend two sessions a week on red topics, starting with number and algebra, because almost everything else builds on them.
- One session a week is mixed practice: ten short questions from anywhere, no notes.
- On Higher, make sure algebraic fractions, rearranging formulae and quadratics are solid before Christmas.

**Phase 2: January to February half term (about 7 weeks). Mocks and gap filling.**

- Treat your mock exams as data. Go through every lost mark and add the topic to your red list.
- Keep one non-calculator session a week, even if your mock was a calculator paper.
- Start full topic tests under time pressure, around 30 minutes each.

**Phase 3: late February to Easter (about 6 weeks). Exam technique.**

- Move from topic practice to full past papers, one a week, under timed conditions.
- Mark them yourself with the official mark scheme straight away, while you still remember your thinking.
- Rewrite any question you lost three or more marks on, a week later, without looking at your old answer.

**Phase 4: after Easter to 14 May (about 4 weeks). Paper 1 focus.**

- Two full non-calculator papers a week.
- Short daily drills on arithmetic, fractions and estimation, five to ten minutes.
- Sleep and routine start to matter more than extra hours now.

**Phase 5: 15 May to 27 May. Paper 2 window.**

- Switch to calculator papers. Do at least three full ones in this window.
- Keep revising other subjects too, but give maths a short session most days.

**Phase 6: 28 May to 14 June. Paper 3 window.**

- Go back to your red list one last time. Anything still red gets a focused session.
- Finish with two or three full calculator papers, then ease off in the last two days.

If you want help building something like this from your own topic list, our guide to [exam prep with Astra AI](https://astra-ai.co/blog/exam-prep-wtih-astra-ai/) shows how a study plan can be set up around a fixed exam date.

## How to use official past papers and mark schemes

Past papers are the best revision resource you have, because they're written by the same people who write your real exam. AQA and Pearson both publish past papers and mark schemes on their websites, and your teacher may have more recent ones through the school.

Some ground rules that make them far more useful:

1. **Sit them properly.** Timer on, phone in another room, the right equipment. A paper done in bits with breaks tells you very little.
2. **Mark with the official mark scheme.** Look at where method marks are given. You can often pick up marks for a correct method even when your final answer is wrong, so always show your working.
3. **Read the examiner reports.** These explain where students commonly lost marks. They're a quick way to spot traps such as forgetting units or rounding too early.
4. **Keep a mistakes log.** Write the question, the topic, what went wrong and the correct method. Read it back before each new paper.
5. **Don't burn through them too early.** Save at least four or five full sets for the final weeks, so you still have fresh papers when it counts.

Spread your papers across Foundation or Higher as appropriate. If you're on the Higher borderline at grade 4 or 5, the first half of Higher papers is often the most useful practice.

## When you get stuck

Everyone hits topics that won't click. The trick is not to lose a whole week to one of them.

**Your teacher** is still your best first stop. Bring a specific question, not "I don't get vectors". Most teachers are glad to help a student who has clearly tried.

**Friends and revision groups** work well for explaining things to each other. If you can teach a method to someone else, you really know it.

**An AI tutor** helps in the moments when you're on your own at 9pm with a question you can't crack. Astra AI, which we build, tutors step by step, asks you questions back and checks your understanding. The answer is the last thing you get, not the first. You can start free, no card required. Astra AI Plus unlocks unlimited tutoring, mock exams and podcasts. For most students it can replace a private tutor, though not for every student. If you're comparing options, our guide to the [best AI tutor](https://astra-ai.co/blog/best-ai-tutor/) covers what to look for, and there's a separate round-up of the [best AI math tutor](https://astra-ai.co/blog/the-best-ai-math-tutor/) tools.

**When time is very short**, don't panic and don't cram new topics the night before a paper. Our piece on [studying the night before an exam](https://astra-ai.co/blog/studying-the-night-before-an-exam/) explains what actually helps in the last 24 hours.

One last thing: your revision timetable is a guide, not a contract. If you're ill for a week or a topic takes longer than planned, move things around and keep going. Consistency over seven months beats a perfect plan you abandon in November. You can find more ideas on our [exam prep](https://astra-ai.co/exam-prep/) page.

## Frequently asked questions

### When are the GCSE maths exams in 2027?

For AQA and Pearson Edexcel, Paper 1 (non-calculator) is on Friday 14 May 2027, Paper 2 (calculator) on Thursday 27 May and Paper 3 (calculator) on Monday 14 June. All three are morning papers lasting 1 hour 30 minutes, and Foundation and Higher sit on the same days. If you sit OCR, check its own timetable.

### When should I start revising for GCSE maths?

Starting in the autumn of Year 11 gives you time to fix weak topics before mocks and still leave several weeks for full timed past papers in spring. If you start later, keep the past paper phase and shorten the early topic review.

### How many hours a week should I revise maths for GCSE?

There is no official number. Three or four focused sessions a week of 30 to 45 minutes, plus one longer weekend session, is a realistic plan for many students. Consistency matters more than long sessions.

### Where can I find GCSE maths past papers?

AQA and Pearson Edexcel publish past papers, mark schemes and examiner reports on their websites. Your teacher may also have recent papers that are not public yet. Mark each paper with the official mark scheme straight after you sit it.

# The best AI for physics: pick by topic, then check the answer

> The best AI for physics depends on your topic and level: a step-by-step tutor to set up the problem, a calculator to check the number, a simulation to see what should happen. We compare Astra AI, Wolfram|Alpha, PhET, ChatGPT study mode and Khanmigo from their own pages, then give you seven physics checks to run on any AI answer.

## The short answer

There is no single best AI for physics. The best AI for physics homework is the one that matches your topic and level, and whose answer survives a few physics checks. A tool that is great at crunching a lens equation can still get the direction of a magnetic force wrong. So pick by topic first, then check every answer before you copy anything into your notebook.

This guide gives you both: a quick route by topic and level, short notes on five tools, and seven checks you can run on any AI answer, whichever tool wrote it.

## How we chose

We looked at what each tool says about itself on its own website or help center, checked on 9 October 2026. We did not run a test with scores, and there is no ranking here. The tools are grouped by the job they do. Prices and plans change and can differ by country, so treat them as a snapshot.

**Astra AI is our product.** It is in the list under the same rules as the others, with its downsides.

## Pick by topic and level

### Mechanics: forces, motion and projectiles

This is where most homework lives: blocks on ramps, cars braking, balls thrown off cliffs. The physics is usually not hard. The mistakes come from a missing force, a sign that flips halfway through, or a component taken with sine instead of cosine.

- Use a tutor that makes you draw the free-body diagram and set an axis before any equation.
- Use PhET's free Forces and Motion: Basics or Projectile Motion simulation when you want to see what the numbers mean.
- Use Wolfram|Alpha to double-check a final number once your own setup is right.

### Circuits, electricity and magnetism

Before Ohm's law, someone has to decide what is in series and what is in parallel. That step is easy to get wrong, for you and for an AI. Magnetic forces add a second trap: the direction comes from a cross product or a right-hand rule, and a sentence like "the force points up" means nothing without axes.

- Build the circuit in PhET's Circuit Construction Kit: DC and see if the current matches your answer.
- When you use any chatbot, ask it to name the series and parallel parts before it calculates.
- Do right-hand-rule directions yourself, with your hand, and compare.

### Waves and optics

Wave speed, frequency and wavelength, lenses and mirrors, refraction. Most questions are one or two formulas, but the sign rules for lenses differ between textbooks, so a correct-looking answer can still use a convention your teacher doesn't.

- PhET's Wave on a String and Bending Light simulations are good for building intuition.
- Wolfram|Alpha has worked examples for the thin lens equation and diffraction.
- Tell the AI which sign convention your class uses.

### Modern physics and calculus-based university courses

Photon energy, relativity and early quantum topics at school, or calculus-based mechanics and electromagnetism at university. At this level the algebra gets longer, so skipped steps hide more mistakes. Ask for the derivation in symbols first and plug in numbers last. If your course is algebra-based, say so, or you may get an answer full of integrals you were never taught.

## Seven checks to run on any AI answer

These come from the mistakes physics teachers see every week. Use them on any tool's answer, including ours.

1. **Units and dimensions.** Every line should carry units, and the final unit must make sense. For v = √(2gh), the units are √(m/s² × m) = m/s. That is a speed, so the formula at least has the right shape.
2. **A free-body diagram before any force equation.** For a block sliding down a 30° ramp with friction coefficient 0.2, the answer should list weight, normal force and friction before writing F = ma. Then a = g(sin 30° - 0.2 × cos 30°) = 9.81 × (0.5 - 0.173) ≈ 3.2 m/s². If friction or the normal force is missing, stop there.
3. **A stated axis and sign convention.** A ball rolls off a 20 m cliff at 5 m/s. Choose down as positive, and it lands after t = √(2h/g) = √(40/9.81) ≈ 2.0 s, about 10 m from the base. An answer that mixes "up is positive" with g = +9.81 m/s² will give nonsense.
4. **Vector direction.** For a launch at 20 m/s and 30° above the horizontal, the horizontal part is 20 × cos 30° ≈ 17.3 m/s and the vertical part is 20 × sin 30° = 10 m/s. For magnetic forces, the answer must say which way the force points and why: a proton moving along +x in a field along +z feels a force along -y.
5. **Circuit layout before Ohm's law.** A 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor in parallel make 2 Ω, not 9 Ω. A quick check: a parallel combination is always smaller than the smallest resistor. On 12 V that is 6 A from the battery, not about 1.3 A.
6. **Order of magnitude.** On the 30° ramp, the acceleration has to be less than g × sin 30° ≈ 4.9 m/s², because friction slows the block down. 3.2 m/s² passes. A thrown ball landing 2 km away does not.
7. **No skipped algebra.** The answer should rearrange in symbols first (from h = ½gt² to t = √(2h/g)) and only then put in numbers. If a number appears out of nowhere, ask where it came from.

## Where AI still trips on physics

A 2026 study in the journal Physics Education, "How well do AI systems solve AP physics?", gave the algebra-based AP Physics 1 and 2 free-response questions from 2015 to 2025 to four widely accessible AI systems: ChatGPT 4.1 mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude 4.0 Sonnet and DeepSeek R1. Three physics experts graded the answers with the official College Board scoring guidelines. The average scores were fairly high, between 82% and 92% depending on the model and the exam. But the authors found the same kinds of mistakes in all four: misreading diagrams and graphs, drawing graphs wrong, reasoning wrongly about vector direction, circuit topology errors, partial or misleading explanations, and trouble with three-dimensional ideas like the right-hand rule. Those were exam questions and specific model versions, so the scores are a snapshot, not a grade for every chatbot today.

The mistakes match the checks above. To get better answers:

- Describe the diagram in words: what is connected to what, which way each arrow points, where the axis is.
- Give every number with its unit.
- Say your level: algebra-based school physics or calculus-based university physics.
- Ask for the setup first and the numbers last.

It is built into Khan Academy's content library, so you can get help on its exercises, videos and articles, and it covers elementary school through college in almost any academic subject, including math, science, coding, history and humanities. You can talk to it instead of typing, and it can read its responses aloud. For learners and parents it costs \$4 a month or \$44 a year, sales tax not included. The Khan Academy library itself stays free.

_Drawback:_ per its FAQ, buyers must be 18 or older, live in the US and have a US billing address. Under-18s need a parent to sign up, and a parent account can add up to 10 children. Classroom access only comes through school or district partnerships.

### Gemini with Guided Learning (Google)

In August 2025 Google added a mode called Guided Learning to the Gemini app and said it was rolling out to everyone. Google describes it as breaking problems down step by step and adapting explanations so you understand the "how" and "why" instead of getting a quick answer. Gemini's help center still explains how to switch it on at gemini.google.com and says the learning tools are reaching the mobile app gradually. Its students page adds study notebooks built from your uploaded course materials, personalized quizzes and Gemini Live for real-time conversations. Gemini's plans page lists a Free plan at \$0 a month with a Google Account, plus paid Google AI Plus, Google AI Pro and Google AI Ultra plans.

_Drawback:_ it is a general-purpose assistant rather than a school product, and which features you get depends on the plan. Google's paid AI plans are for ages 18 and up. The free one-year student offer is only for eligible US college students aged 18 and over, must be redeemed by 31 December 2026 and needs a payment method; Google says AI Pro then renews at \$19.99 a month unless you cancel.

### Quizlet

Quizlet's AI tools page lists AI Homework Help, which it describes as AI-powered tutoring with alternate solution methods, deeper concept breakdowns and personalized practice. The same page lists AI practice tests from your notes, a study guide generator for notes, slides or PDFs, a PDF summarizer and an AI flashcard maker. Quizlet says you can start with some AI features for free, and that more advanced capabilities are in Quizlet Plus.

_Drawback:_ the pages we could read don't show a price for Quizlet Plus, and they don't list which AI features are free. Most tools on that page turn your material into tests, guides and flashcards, so it leans toward revision more than a long back-and-forth about one problem.

### Brainly

Brainly's homepage describes AI homework help and test prep for every subject in grades 7 to 12. It says it chooses between a full explanation, a nudge or a question back, depending on whether the student is missing something or trying to hand the work over. In its Worksheets, the next step stays locked until the current one is right. A learning advisor keeps parents in the loop, you can add a weekly human tutor, and there is a 100% money-back guarantee for the first 30 days. Its help center lists Brainly Plus and Brainly Tutor plans, monthly or annual.

_Drawback:_ the pages we checked don't show a price. Brainly's help center says pricing varies by platform and points to its subscription page. The homepage is written for parents of teens in grades 7 to 12, so it is not aimed at university students.

## When a human tutor is the better pick

An AI tutor is there whenever you open it and doesn't mind the same question three times. What it can't do is hold you accountable the way a person can, and it can get a step wrong. A human tutor is the better pick when motivation is the problem, when written work needs a human reader, or when a younger child needs a person on the call.

- Wyzant is a marketplace: you check tutors' credentials and reviews, see whether they have had a background check, message them before booking, and pay after the lesson. Its Good Fit Guarantee covers the first hour if the fit is wrong.
- Preply offers a 25- or 50-minute trial lesson, then a subscription of 1 to 5 hours a week. If the trial disappoints, it says you can switch tutors for free or get a full refund. Its how-it-works page is written around language learning.
- Varsity Tutors offers private 1-on-1 tutoring, weekly live classes, and practice tests and diagnostics. Its homepage shows no prices.

A practical setup is one human session a week plus an AI tutor between sessions. Bring the mistakes you made with the AI to the human session, so the tutor spends time on what you actually got wrong. For what research says about the two, see [traditional tutoring vs AI tutoring](https://astra-ai.co/blog/traditional-tutoring/).

## Where Astra AI fits

Astra AI is our product, so weigh this section accordingly. It fits when the main need is understanding and practice from your own class material: a step explained at your level, quizzes from your notes, and a plan to a test date through [Exam Prep](https://astra-ai.co/exam-prep/).

It doesn't fit when you need a person: a younger child who needs supervision, essays that need a human reader, or a student who won't study unless someone is waiting for them. Unlimited tutoring needs Astra AI Plus, and like any AI tutor it can make mistakes, so check tricky answers against your textbook or teacher.

## How to test an AI tutor in one to two weeks

1. Write one goal you can check, such as "solve quadratic word problems without hints" or "explain photosynthesis in my own words."
2. Pick one or two AI tutors from the list and use them only on that week's real assignments.
3. After every session, do one fresh problem alone. If you can solve it without help, the AI taught you something; if you can't, it may have done too much of the work for you.
4. Decide at the end. Keep it if you hit the goal or are clearly closer and used it without being chased. Drop it if sessions felt useful but you still can't do the fresh problem, or if a paid plan costs more than your use justifies.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the best AI tutor for students?

There is no single best AI tutor; it depends on how you study. Khanmigo suits US families who want an AI that won't give answers away. Gemini with Guided Learning is a free general option. Quizlet fits flashcard and practice-test learners, Brainly is built for grades 7 to 12 with parent updates, and Astra AI (our product) teaches from your own notes toward a test date.

Yes, several let you start free. Gemini has a free plan, and Google says Guided Learning rolled out to everyone. Khanmigo is paid, but the Khan Academy library is free.

### Is an AI tutor as good as a human tutor?

It depends on the problem. An AI tutor is strong for explanations on demand and extra practice. A human tutor is better at keeping you accountable, reading longer written work and noticing when you are lost. A practical setup is one human session a week with an AI tutor in between.

### What is the best tutoring platform?

It depends on whether you need an AI or a person. An AI tutor like the five above suits explanations and practice whenever you sit down to study. A human tutoring platform suits accountability and feedback on written work: Wyzant lets you check tutors' credentials and reviews and you pay only after a lesson, Preply starts with a 25- or 50-minute trial lesson and then a subscription based on how many hours a week you want, and Varsity Tutors offers private 1-on-1 tutoring and weekly live classes.

### Will an AI tutor just give my child the answers?

Several are designed not to. Khan Academy says Khanmigo never gives the answer, Brainly says it can ask a question back and keeps the next step locked until the current one is right, and Astra AI asks questions back and gives the answer last. # Best Study Apps for Students: Pick by What You Need to Do

> The best study app depends on the job: an app that explains step by step for homework, spaced-repetition flashcards for memorising, and a plan with practice tests for a dated exam. Two apps usually cover it, one tutor-style and one for practice, tested for a week.

## Short answer: there is no single best study app

The best study app depends on the job in front of you. Understanding a new topic needs an app that explains and asks you questions back. Memorising vocabulary or formulas needs spaced repetition. A test on a fixed date needs a plan and practice under test conditions. Checking a math answer needs a solver, used after you have tried the problem yourself.

For most students that means two apps, not five: one tutor-style app for understanding and one flashcard or practice app for memory. Pick them by the job you have this week, then give them a seven-day trial (steps at the end).

| Your job this week                          | What to look for                                  | Apps to check                      |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Understand a topic, get unstuck on homework | Step-by-step help that asks you for the next step | Khanmigo, Astra AI                 |
| Memorise terms, vocabulary, formulas        | Flashcards that schedule or adapt your reviews    | Anki, Quizlet                      |
| Prepare for a test on a date                | A plan that ends on the date, practice tests      | Astra AI Exam Prep, Quizlet        |
| Check a math answer after trying it         | Step-by-step solutions                            | Photomath, Symbolab, Google Lens   |
| Turn your own notes into practice           | Upload of your own material                       | Astra AI Exam Prep, Anki (by hand) |

## How we chose the apps on this page

We used five questions, in this order:

1. **Does it teach or only answer?** An app that shows the full solution at once is useful for checking, not for learning.
2. **Does it work from your own materials?** Your teacher's notes and slides are closer to your test than a generic lesson.
3. **What is free today?** Taken from each vendor's own page, checked on 8 October 2026. If a vendor doesn't publish a price, we say so instead of guessing.
4. **Does it fit your course or exam?**
5. **Who is it built for?** Some apps have age or country limits that rule them out before you start.

This is not a ranking. We did not run a lab test, and there are no scores. Each app gets one fact from its own site and one drawback. **Astra AI is our product.** It is listed under the same rules and gets a drawback too.

## Understand a topic or get unstuck on homework

When you are stuck, the right app asks you for the next step instead of printing the whole solution. If you want to know how that works in practice, see [what an AI tutor is](https://astra-ai.co/blog/what-is-ai-tutoring/).

**Khanmigo (Khan Academy).** Khan Academy says Khanmigo guides learners to find the answer themselves rather than handing it over, and that the Khan Academy content library stays free. Khanmigo itself costs \$4 a month or \$44 a year for learners and parents.
_Drawback:_ according to its FAQ, buying it requires being 18 or older, living in the United States and having a US billing address. Under-18s get access through a parent's account.
_Use it when:_ you live in the US and already learn with Khan Academy's free lessons. More in our [Khan Academy for math](https://astra-ai.co/blog/khan-academy-for-math/) review.

**Astra AI (our product).** You photograph a question and the AI tutor walks you through the solution step by step, and you can ask a follow-up whenever a step isn't clear. You can start free without a card.
_Drawback:_ the free plan doesn't include unlimited tutoring, so long homework sessions can run into the limit.
_Use it when:_ you need help across several subjects and want to question each step.

## Memorise: flashcards and spaced repetition

Flashcards work best when a card comes back just before you would forget it. Anki schedules that for you; Quizlet's Learn mode adapts to what you already know.

**Anki.** You rate how well you remembered each card, and Anki schedules the next review for when you are most likely to forget it. The computer version, AnkiDroid for Android and the AnkiWeb sync service are free. AnkiMobile, the official iPhone app, is a paid purchase.
_Drawback:_ you build or import your decks yourself, and Anki won't explain the material. It assumes you already understand it.
_Use it when:_ you have a lot of facts to keep for months, such as vocabulary, anatomy terms or formulas.

**Quizlet.** Quizlet's Learn mode builds a study path from your goal and how well you already know a set.
_Drawback:_ per Quizlet's help centre, Learn is part of the Quizlet Plus subscription. Without it you can try one free Learn session. Students in a teacher's Quizlet class get Learn and Test free for that class's sets.
_Use it when:_ your class already shares Quizlet sets, or you want ready-made question types without building cards.

## Prepare for a test on a fixed date

Work backwards from the date: what is on the test, how many days you have, and when you will do a full practice run. If the test is tomorrow, read [how to study the night before an exam](https://astra-ai.co/blog/studying-the-night-before-an-exam/) instead.

**Astra AI Exam Prep (our product).** You upload notes, PDFs, past tests or worksheets, set the test date, and Exam Prep builds a study plan that ends on that date. Along the way you get exercises, quizzes, flashcards and podcasts, and at the end you can sit a timed mock exam or practise answering out loud. Details on the [Exam Prep](https://astra-ai.co/exam-prep/) page.
_Drawback:_ the plan can only be as good as what you upload. Thin notes give a thin plan, and mock exams and podcasts need Astra AI Plus.
_Use it when:_ you have real class materials and a date.

**Quizlet (Learn and Test).** If your teacher shares sets, Learn and Test can turn them into practice before the test, with the subscription limits above.

Whichever app you use, do at least one full practice run under time pressure before the real thing, and keep a short list of the mistakes you made.

## Check a math answer after you've tried it

Solvers are good at one job: telling you whether your answer and method match. **Photomath** lets you scan a problem, including word problems, and shows step-by-step explanations. Its site lists a free Basic plan and a paid plan at \$9.99 a month or \$69.99 a year (USD). **Symbolab** shows step-by-step solutions for typed or photographed problems and has practice quizzes. **Google Lens** offers step-by-step homework help by finding explainers, videos and web results for math and science questions.

_Drawback for all three:_ the solution is one tap away, so it is easy to copy instead of learn. Try the problem first, then check. For course-by-course math picks, see [the best AI math tutor](https://astra-ai.co/blog/the-best-ai-math-tutor/) and our [Photomath alternative](https://astra-ai.co/blog/photomath-alternative/) comparison. For chemistry, see [the best AI for chemistry](https://astra-ai.co/blog/the-best-ai-chemistry-tutor/).

## Turn your own notes or slides into practice

Of all the jobs here, this one sits closest to what your teacher will actually test.

- **Astra AI Exam Prep** turns uploaded notes, PDFs and past tests into lessons, quizzes and flashcards.
- **Anki** does it by hand: you write the cards from your notes. Slower, but writing the question is already study.

We could not confirm on other vendors' own pages, on 8 October 2026, that they build practice from files you upload, so they are not listed for this job.

After a session, cover the solution, take a fresh problem of the same type and solve it without the app. If you can, the app taught you something. If you can't, it gave you an answer and you still need the method. Run this test at the end of every session during your trial week; it tells you more than any feature list.

Astra AI is our product, so read this section with that in mind. It fits best when you have your own class materials and a test date, and you want explanations and practice in one place across several subjects: a photographed homework question one evening, an [Exam Prep](https://astra-ai.co/exam-prep/) plan built from your notes the next. It runs on iPhone, iPad and Android via the [mobile app](https://astra-ai.co/mobile-app/) as well as in the browser.

It is not the right pick for everything. If all you need is vocabulary drill, a dedicated flashcard app like Anki is simpler. If you need a person who holds you accountable, an AI tutor won't replace that. The free plan limits tutoring, the Plus price is only shown inside the app, and like any AI tutor it can get a step wrong, so compare tricky answers with your textbook or teacher.

## How to pick in one week

1. Name the job in one sentence, for example: "biology test on the 20th, chapters 4-6."
2. Pick one app for that job from the sections above, plus a flashcard app if the test has a lot to memorise.
3. Use it for five days, 20-30 minutes a day, and finish each session with the cover test.
4. Decide on day seven. Keep the app if you can solve fresh problems without it and you actually opened it every day. Drop it if you mostly copied answers or kept hitting a paywall you don't want to pay for.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is there a free study app that actually helps?

Yes, if you match it to the job. Anki is free on computers and Android and handles spaced-repetition flashcards. Khan Academy's lesson library is free. Astra AI lets you start free without a card, with limited tutoring. Check each vendor's own page for current limits, because free tiers change.

### Is using an AI study app cheating?

Using an AI app to understand a topic, practise or check your own work is studying. Submitting answers it wrote for graded work usually breaks school rules. Your teacher's or school's policy decides where the line is, so check it, and use the app to explain steps rather than to produce what you hand in.

### Flashcards or an AI tutor: which should I use first?

Start with a tutor-style app when you don't understand the material yet; flashcards can't explain anything. Once a topic makes sense, move the key facts and formulas into flashcards so you keep them until the test. Many students use both in the same week.

### What should a good exam prep app do?

It should plan backwards from your test date, give you practice questions on the topics that will be tested, and let you do a timed practice run before the real exam. Apps that build practice from your own class notes stay closest to what your teacher will ask.
